Mixing-period tag recaptures in MULTIFAN-CL: a simulation study

Comparing tag_flags(i,2) settings against likelihood-based alternatives

Published

August 5, 2026

Executive summary

MULTIFAN-CL handles tag recaptures during the mixing period by inverting the observed returns rather than predicting them. tag_flags(i,2) selects the target: the default raises reported returns by the assumed reporting rate and removes that many tags; the alternative removes the reported returns at face value, which amounts to assuming complete reporting. Neither scores the mixing-period data in the likelihood, so under both settings those data fix the tagged population state with no uncertainty attached and no ability for the model to object. Both treatments are wrong, and the choice cannot be avoided in any model that fits to tags. This study simulates both, together with two likelihood-based alternatives, across reporting-rate misspecification, mixing-period length, tagged-fish availability during mixing, a realistic clumped reporting process, and release-group size.

The default is unbiased under three conditions and not otherwise: the assumed reporting rate is correct, the survival floor is not engaging, and release groups are large. Given those, it recovers \(F\) across every combination of mixing length and tagged-fish availability tested, which is a genuine strength — the deterministic inversion never needs to know how available tagged fish were during mixing. The alternative is biased even when everything else is specified perfectly, but its bias is at least largely predictable. It is governed by \(\psi\), the proportion of each release group recaptured within tag_flags(i,1) periods of release: a few percent at \(\psi = 0.05\), roughly a third of \(F\) at \(\psi = 0.3\), half or more by \(\psi = 0.5\). That fraction is computable from the .tag file in advance, provided the reported returns are raised by the assumed reporting rate first.

Where the default’s conditions fail, the errors are consequential and hard to see. When the realised catch fraction in a mixing period exceeds roughly four-fifths of the assumed reporting rate, posfun silently caps the removal, the default then under-removes, and \(F\) is biased downward and biomass upward — the same direction as the alternative it is supposed to improve on. At small release-group sizes the inversion’s convexity puts weight in the upper tail of \(F\) instead: a minority of groups return estimates many times the truth while the median at the same cell says nothing at all, so this second failure is invisible to the diagnostics an assessment normally reports. Nor do the two settings bound the problem between them. Because the assumed reporting rate is below one, the default always removes more tags and always returns the larger \(F\), so the pair is structurally one-sided: it cannot contain the truth when the assumed rate is too high, and where it does contain it the interval is often wider than the quantity being estimated. Running both as grid levels spans an assumption without bounding anything. Note too that the assumed reporting rate is itself the first-order channel in most configurations examined — larger than the flag choice — so a biomass shift should not be attributed to the flag without knowing what the reporting rates did.

This matters now because reporting-rate estimates are moving downward. The tag-seeding analysis prepared for the 2026 assessments (SC22-SA-IP-05) puts the purse seine reporting-rate priors for bigeye at means of 0.496 to 0.528 across regions 2 to 4, between 15 and 24 per cent below what the 2023 assessments would have used under the same region and fishery definitions. The survival-floor condition is reached routinely at an assumed rate of 0.2 and is reachable at 0.5 when tagged fish are highly available during mixing, so the bigeye assessment sits at the boundary of the default’s second condition rather than comfortably inside it, and it arrived there by moving in the direction that makes the condition harder to satisfy.

There is a treatment that removes the dilemma, and it is not available to the 2026 assessments. Predicting mixing-period returns and scoring them in the likelihood, with the reporting rate free to move against its tag-seeding prior, puts those data on the same footing as post-mixing returns and inverts nothing. This study implements that treatment (forward_X) alongside the two flag settings, and it recovers \(F\) under the reporting-rate misspecification that biases both of them. MULTIFAN-CL cannot currently do this: the mixing-period returns do not enter the tag likelihood under either flag setting, so it is a redevelopment request to the MULTIFAN-CL team rather than a configuration choice. It is also not free. With many small release groups it was the least precise of the four estimators tested here — estimating the reporting rate, the availability multiplier and \(F\) together needs information a fragmented tagging programme may not carry. That finding comes with a caveat: the prior imposed on the reporting rate in these runs is far looser than the tag-seeding priors an assessment would use, so an unknown share of the imprecision belongs to the prior rather than to the estimator, and the comparison should be re-run before the finding is leaned on.

In the meantime the most useful response is not to pick a setting but to bound how much the tag data are driving the answer at all. We recommend that a configuration omitting tagging data — with the spatial information instead carried by a spatially implicit fleets-as-areas structure — be included in the structural uncertainty grid, and treated as a more informative addition to it than either flag setting. If it produces similar stock status, the mixing-period treatment is a second-order concern and can be documented as such; if it does not, the difference is attributable to a model component that is defective under either setting. It also answers a question managers ask directly: how much of this result depends on the tagging programme? Two of the default’s three conditions — whether the survival floor is liable to engage, and whether release groups are large enough for the large-sample argument to apply — can be checked in advance against the .tag file and the flag settings, and What to check in an assessment that fits to tags sets out how. The third, the correctness of the assumed reporting rate, is the quantity under dispute and cannot be settled from inside the model.

A note on scope. The tag-free, spatially implicit fleets-as-areas recommendation is a reasoned position, not a simulated result — nothing here tests a spatial model or a fleets-as-areas configuration. What the simulation supports is the narrower claim that both tag_flags(i,2) settings are biased, that their biases are not bounding, and that the conditions under which each fails are identifiable in advance.

Scope and methods

Purpose

MULTIFAN-CL handles tag recaptures differently before and after the mixing period.

After mixing, the tagged population is projected forward with the population fishing mortality, predicted returns are formed as \(E[R] = X \times C\) (reporting rate times true recaptures), and observed returns are scored in the likelihood. Nothing is inverted.

During mixing, do_newton_raphson_for_tags() instead solves deterministically for a tag-specific \(F\) such that the removal equals a target derived from the observed returns. The flag tag_flags(i,2) chooses the target:

Setting Target removal Interpretation
tag_flags(i,2) = 0 (default) \(R_{obs} / X\) reported returns raised for non-reporting
tag_flags(i,2) = 1 \(R_{obs}\) reported returns taken at face value

Mixing-period returns contribute nothing to the likelihood under either setting. They have full authority over the tagged population state and zero influence on parameter estimation, with no uncertainty attached.

This vignette runs five experiments.

Experiment A holds the assumed reporting rate fixed at 0.5 — the value the analyst supplies, whether from tag seeding or by assumption — and varies the true reporting rate above, at, and below it. That is the realistic framing: you choose what you assume, and the error runs in a direction you cannot see.

Experiment B adds two further dimensions that the assessment configuration controls directly: the length of the mixing period, tag_flags(i,1), at 2, 3 and 4 quarters; and the relative availability of tagged fish during mixing, including the case where tagged fish are more vulnerable than the general population rather than less. The latter is arguably the more realistic case for purse-seine fisheries, where tags are released from fishing vessels into concentrated effort.

Experiment C replaces the clean observation model with a realistic one: small release groups, stochastic recaptures, and reporting clumped at the trip level. This is what makes the survival-floor failure mode reachable at ordinary fishing mortalities, and it identifies the assumed reporting rate as the parameter that controls it.

Experiment D reparameterises the flag1 result by the fraction of a release group recaptured during mixing, which turns the bias into something an analyst can look up from their own .tag file.

Experiment E isolates release-group size, to test whether the residual scatter flag0 shows at high recapture fractions in Experiment D is Monte Carlo noise or a real small-sample property of inverting a noisy target.

The operating model is deliberately stripped down: one fishery, one region, no age structure, no movement, no tag shedding beyond natural mortality. Experiments A and B use a single large release cohort; C and D use several smaller groups sharing one fishing mortality; E uses a single group of varying size, for the reason given in that section. It is not a fisheries model. It isolates the mixing-period mechanism and nothing else.

Setup

Code 
library(data.table)
library(magrittr)
library(ggplot2)

theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 11))
set.seed(20260802)

pal <- c(flag0     = "#D85A30",
         flag1     = "#1D9E75",
         forward   = "#7F77DD",
         forward_X = "#378ADD",
         truth     = "grey30")

# Threshold defining a "gross overshoot" of the deterministic inversion, as a
# multiple of the true F. Used as the primary tail statistic in Experiment E.
# It has to sit far enough above the truth to be unambiguous, far enough below
# the search ceiling to be insensitive to it (the ceilings are at roughly 33x
# and 333x the truth), and low enough to capture sufficient mass for the
# difference across group sizes to be resolvable at the replicate count used.
E_TAIL_MULT <- 5

Formatting helpers. Every number quoted in the prose below is produced by one of these from a fitted object, so the text cannot drift out of step with the results when the design or the replicate count changes.

Code 
# Percentage, signed by default (biases read better with an explicit sign).
fpc <- function(x, digits = 0, signed = TRUE) {
  sprintf(paste0("%", if (signed) "+" else "", ".", digits, "f%%"), 100 * x)
}

# Range of a vector, as a percentage: "-41% to +16%". If both ends format
# identically -- which happens whenever a quantity is constant across the cells
# being summarised -- collapse to the single value, so the prose reads "0%"
# rather than the nonsensical "0% to 0%".
fpc_range <- function(x, digits = 0) {
  lo <- fpc(min(x), digits)
  hi <- fpc(max(x), digits)
  if (identical(lo, hi)) lo else paste0(lo, " to ", hi)
}

fnum <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)

# Range of values already expressed in percentage points: "17-67%". Collapses to
# a single value when both ends round alike, so a quantity that is constant
# across the cells being summarised does not read as the nonsensical "0-0%".
fpp_range <- function(x, digits = 0) {
  lo <- fnum(min(x), digits)
  hi <- fnum(max(x), digits)
  if (identical(lo, hi)) paste0(lo, "%") else paste0(lo, "\u2013", hi, "%")
}

# Monte Carlo standard error of a sample median (normal approximation).
mcse_median <- function(x) 1.2533 * stats::sd(x) / sqrt(length(x))

Operating model

Discrete quarterly steps. Within a period, tagged fish die from fishing and natural causes following Baranov:

\[C_t = \frac{F^T_t}{Z_t}\left(1 - e^{-Z_t}\right) N_t, \qquad N_{t+1} = N_t\, e^{-Z_t}, \qquad Z_t = F^T_t + M\]

During the mixing period, tagged fish have a different availability to the fishery than the general population, so \(F^T_t = \varphi F_t\); afterwards \(\varphi = 1\). Values \(\varphi < 1\) mean tagged fish are harder to catch than average (the assumption implicit in the usual justification for a mixing period); \(\varphi > 1\) means they are easier to catch, which is what happens when effort is concentrated around release sites. Reported returns are a thinned observation of the true recaptures, \(R_t \sim \text{Poisson}(X_{true}\, C_t)\).

Code 
baranov <- function(f, n, m) {
  z <- f + m
  (f / z) * (1 - exp(-z)) * n
}

om <- list(
  N0        = 10000,  # tags released (known exactly)
  Tmax      = 12,     # quarters at liberty
  M         = 0.20,   # natural mortality per quarter
  F_true    = 0.15,   # post-mixing fishing mortality per quarter -- the estimand
  X_assumed = 0.50,   # the reporting rate the analyst supplies -- fixed in every
                      # experiment except C, which varies it deliberately. The
                      # value is the 2026 bigeye purse seine prior mean (see below).
  nmix      = 2,      # baseline mixing periods, i.e. tag_flags(i,1)
  phi       = 0.50    # baseline availability multiplier during mixing
)

simulate_returns <- function(p, X_true, phi = p$phi, nmix = p$nmix) {
  n <- p$N0
  r <- numeric(p$Tmax)
  for (t in seq_len(p$Tmax)) {
    f_t  <- p$F_true * if (t <= nmix) phi else 1
    r[t] <- rpois(1, X_true * baranov(f_t, n, p$M))
    n    <- n * exp(-(f_t + p$M))
  }
  r
}

The assumed reporting rate of 0.50 is not a round number chosen for convenience. The tag-seeding analysis prepared for the 2026 assessments (SC22-SA-IP-05) gives purse seine reporting-rate priors for bigeye with means of 0.496 in region 2, 0.512 in region 3 and 0.528 in region 4, so 0.50 is the operative value for the assessment this work is aimed at and the panels at \(X_{assumed} = 0.5\) elsewhere in this document are the ones to read first. Three qualifications travel with that number and are repeated wherever it is used: those are purse seine fisheries only, so the mapping onto a single-fishery operating model is by analogy; they are penalty distributions rather than fixed values, so a real model estimates the rate against them rather than dividing by a constant; and the region 2 penalty was deliberately halved to reflect additional uncertainty, with the prior not recommended for the Indonesian and Philippine domestic fisheries at all.

The mixing-period step

One function performs the deterministic inversion, and every estimator, every trajectory plot and every diagnostic in this document calls it. This is load-bearing rather than tidiness. If the estimator capped the removal one way — say a hard min(target, 0.99 * n) — and the floor diagnostic used an ADMB-style survival floor, the two would advance the tagged population differently as soon as the cap engaged, and the frequency of floor engagement reported would not be the frequency the estimator actually experienced. A single implementation makes that class of discrepancy impossible by construction.

The floor reproduces the MULTIFAN-CL behaviour qualitatively: survival is not allowed below cut + fringe, the removal is rescaled to whatever the floored survival implies, and a quadratic penalty is accumulated. The defaults match age_flags(118) and (119).

Code 
CUT    <- 0.20   # age_flags(118) analogue
FRINGE <- 0.02   # age_flags(119) analogue -- survival floor is CUT + FRINGE
PENWT  <- 1e3    # penalty weight; see note below and the Limitations

# ADMB posfun: smooth floor with a quadratic penalty.
posfun <- function(x, eps) {
  if (x >= eps) return(c(y = x, pen = 0))
  c(y = eps / (2 - x / eps), pen = (x - eps)^2)
}

# Newton solver for the tag F. Mirrors do_newton_raphson_for_tags() and is
# faster than uniroot().
solve_F_newton <- function(target, n, m, iter = 25) {
  if (target <= 0) return(0)
  u <- min(target / n, 0.999)
  f <- -log(1 - u)                       # exponential-approximation start
  for (i in seq_len(iter)) {
    z  <- f + m
    e  <- exp(-z)
    g  <- (f / z) * (1 - e) * n - target
    dg <- n * ((m * (1 - e)) / z^2 + (f / z) * e)
    f  <- max(f - g / dg, 1e-10)
  }
  f
}

# THE single mixing-period step. Returns the realised target, the F that
# achieves it, the penalty incurred, and whether the survival floor engaged.
mix_step <- function(r_t, n, p, mode, cut = CUT, fringe = FRINGE) {
  target  <- if (mode == "flag0") r_t / p$X_assumed else r_t
  surv    <- 1 - target / n
  floored <- surv < cut + fringe
  pen     <- 0
  if (floored) {
    pf     <- posfun(surv - fringe, cut)
    surv   <- fringe + pf[["y"]]
    pen    <- pf[["pen"]]
    target <- n * (1 - surv)
  }
  list(target = target, f = solve_F_newton(target, n, p$M),
       pen = pen, floored = floored)
}

Note that for flag0 and flag1 the target depends only on the data, never on a parameter, so the penalty is a constant with respect to the parameter vector and cannot move \(\hat{F}\). This is not a shortcut: it is a faithful analogue of the age_flags(117) < 0 case, in which the rescaling happens with no trace in the objective function. It does mean the penalty in this vignette is a bookkeeping device rather than something the optimiser responds to.

The estimators

All estimate \(F\) on the log scale. They differ only in how the mixing periods are handled. Every one uses X_assumed = 0.5; none is told the true reporting rate, and none is told \(\varphi\).

Label Mixing-period removal Mixing returns in likelihood? Free parameters
flag0 \(R_t / X_{assumed}\), solved deterministically no \(\log F\)
flag1 \(R_t\), solved deterministically no \(\log F\)
forward predicted from \(\varphi F\) yes \(\log F\), \(\log \varphi\)
forward_X predicted from \(\varphi F\) yes \(\log F\), \(\log \varphi\), \(\text{logit}\,X\)

forward_X additionally estimates the reporting rate under a lognormal prior centred on the assumed value — the analogue of a tag-seeding prior via fish_flags(i,35) and (i,36).

flag0 and flag1 never estimate \(\varphi\); they do not need to, because they solve for whatever mixing-period \(F\) reproduces their target removal. Whether that makes them robust to \(\varphi\) or merely indifferent to it is one of the questions Experiment B answers.

Because the flag modes have a single free parameter, they are optimised with optimize() rather than being handed a three-element simplex with two exactly flat directions. This is both faster and more reliable than handing them to a general-purpose optimiser.

Code 
nll_tag <- function(par, r, p, mode, nmix = p$nmix, prior_sd = 0.4) {
  f_pop <- exp(par[1])
  phi   <- if (mode %in% c("forward", "forward_X")) exp(par[2]) else 1
  x     <- if (mode == "forward_X") plogis(par[3]) else p$X_assumed

  n   <- p$N0
  nll <- 0

  for (t in seq_len(p$Tmax)) {
    premix <- t <= nmix

    if (premix && mode %in% c("flag0", "flag1")) {
      # Deterministic inversion. No likelihood contribution; the penalty is
      # constant in `par` (see note above).
      st  <- mix_step(r[t], n, p, mode)
      f_t <- st$f
      nll <- nll + PENWT * st$pen
    } else {
      # Forward prediction, scored against the data.
      f_t <- if (premix) f_pop * phi else f_pop
      mu  <- x * baranov(f_t, n, p$M) + 1e-10
      nll <- nll - dpois(r[t], mu, log = TRUE)
    }
    n <- n * exp(-(f_t + p$M))
  }

  if (mode == "forward_X") {
    nll <- nll + 0.5 * ((log(x) - log(p$X_assumed)) / prior_sd)^2
  }
  nll
}

LOGF_INT      <- c(log(1e-3), log(5))    # search interval for the 1-D flag modes
LOGF_INT_WIDE <- c(log(1e-5), log(50))   # stress interval, used in Experiment E
BOUND_TOL     <- 1e-3                    # log-scale tolerance for endpoint contact

# The flag modes are optimised over a bounded interval, so `optimize()` always
# returns a value and a convergence code would be meaningless for them. The
# meaningful diagnostic is whether the returned estimate is sitting on an
# endpoint: if it is, the number reported is a property of the search interval
# rather than of the data, and any statistic sensitive to the tail of the F-hat
# distribution has to be checked against it. Replicates that hit a bound are
# retained in every summary below, not dropped -- discarding them would remove
# exactly the behaviour being characterised -- but they are counted and reported.
at_bound_lf <- function(lf, interval, tol = BOUND_TOL) {
  any(abs(lf - interval) < tol)
}

fit_one <- function(r, p, mode, nmix = p$nmix, interval = LOGF_INT) {
  mode <- as.character(mode)[1L]

  if (mode %in% c("flag0", "flag1")) {
    opt <- stats::optimize(
      function(lf) nll_tag(c(lf, 0, 0), r, p, mode, nmix),
      interval = interval, tol = 1e-10)
    return(data.table(F_hat = exp(opt$minimum), phi_hat = NA_real_,
                      X_hat = p$X_assumed, conv = 0L,
                      at_bound = at_bound_lf(opt$minimum, interval)))
  }

  opt <- stats::optim(
    par = c(log(0.10), 0, qlogis(p$X_assumed)),
    fn = function(par) nll_tag(par, r, p, mode, nmix),
    method = "Nelder-Mead",
    control = list(maxit = 5000, reltol = 1e-12))

  data.table(
    F_hat    = exp(opt$par[1]),
    phi_hat  = exp(opt$par[2]),
    X_hat    = if (mode == "forward_X") plogis(opt$par[3]) else p$X_assumed,
    conv     = opt$convergence,
    at_bound = FALSE)   # unbounded search; `conv` is the diagnostic here
}

A note on what the flag modes can and cannot return. The deterministic inversion solves for whatever mixing-period \(F\) reproduces its target removal, and that target is a noisy observation divided by a fixed constant. When a small release group happens to return an unusually large number of tags in a mixing period, the implied removal can approach the tags available, and the solved \(F\) can be arbitrarily large. The search interval is what stops it running away. That makes the upper endpoint a modelling choice with consequences for any mean, and it is why at_bound is carried through every experiment and why Experiment E repeats its design at LOGF_INT_WIDE as well.

Experiment A: reporting-rate misspecification

The assumed reporting rate is fixed at 0.5. The true rate takes three values, so the assumption is right in one case and wrong in each direction in the others. Mixing length and availability stay at their baseline (nmix = 2, \(\varphi = 0.5\)).

Code 
scenarios <- data.table(
  X_true = c(0.35, 0.50, 0.65),
  case   = factor(c("true < assumed", "true = assumed", "true > assumed"),
                  levels = c("true < assumed", "true = assumed", "true > assumed"))
)

Mechanism: what happens to the tagged population

Before looking at estimates, look at the state. This traces tags at liberty through the mixing period under each treatment, for one realisation per scenario, with \(F\) held at its true value. Plotting the ratio to the true trajectory rather than the trajectory itself is what makes the mechanism visible: on an absolute axis, over an order-of-magnitude decline, the three series are indistinguishable.

Code 
trajectory <- function(r, p, treatment, phi = p$phi, nmix = p$nmix) {
  n   <- p$N0
  out <- numeric(p$Tmax + 1)
  out[1] <- n
  for (t in seq_len(p$Tmax)) {
    premix <- t <= nmix
    if (premix && treatment %in% c("flag0", "flag1")) {
      f_t <- mix_step(r[t], n, p, treatment)$f
    } else {
      f_t <- p$F_true * if (premix) phi else 1   # "truth"
    }
    n <- n * exp(-(f_t + p$M))
    out[t + 1] <- n
  }
  data.table(period = 0:p$Tmax, N = out, treatment = treatment)
}

set.seed(11)
traj <- scenarios[, {
  r <- simulate_returns(om, X_true)
  c("truth", "flag0", "flag1") %>%
    lapply(trajectory, r = r, p = om) %>%
    rbindlist()
}, by = .(case, X_true)]

traj[, treatment := factor(treatment, levels = c("truth", "flag0", "flag1"))]

# Express each treatment relative to the truth within (case, period).
traj[, N_rel := N / N[treatment == "truth"], by = .(case, period)]

ggplot(traj[treatment != "truth"], aes(period, N_rel, colour = treatment)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = om$nmix, linetype = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ case) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, om$Tmax, by = 3)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal) +
  labs(x = "Quarters at liberty", y = "Tags at liberty / truth", colour = NULL,
       subtitle = paste0("Assumed reporting rate = ", om$X_assumed,
                         " in all panels; only the truth changes"))

When the true reporting rate is below what we assume, observed returns are sparse relative to the true recaptures, and flag0 divides by too large a number — it under-removes, so the ratio sits above 1. When the truth is above what we assume, flag0 over-removes. flag1 never raises the returns at all, so it always removes the fewest tags and carries the largest cohort into the informative periods. The flat sections after quarter 2 are the point: the error is created entirely within the mixing period and is then locked in.

Simulation

Code 
n_rep <- 200
modes <- c("flag0", "flag1", "forward", "forward_X")

grid_a <- CJ(rep = seq_len(n_rep), case = scenarios$case, mode = modes,
             sorted = FALSE) %>%
  merge(scenarios, by = "case")

res_a <- grid_a[, {
  # One dataset per (rep, case), shared across estimators via a fixed seed,
  # so the four fits are paired and directly comparable.
  set.seed(as.integer(1e6 * X_true) + rep)
  r <- simulate_returns(om, X_true)
  fit_one(r, om, mode = mode)
}, by = .(rep, case, X_true, mode)]

res_a[, `:=`(mode     = factor(mode, levels = modes),
             rel_bias = F_hat / om$F_true - 1)]
Code 
# Counts flagged fits, not just non-convergent ones: for the bounded 1-D modes
# `conv` is 0 by construction, so a table of `conv != 0` alone would report
# zeros whatever the estimator did.
knitr::kable(
  dcast(res_a[, .(flagged = sum(conv != 0 | at_bound)), by = .(case, mode)],
        case ~ mode, value.var = "flagged"),
  caption = paste0("Experiment A: fits that either failed to converge or ",
                   "returned an estimate on the edge of the search interval, ",
                   "out of ", n_rep, " per cell."))
Experiment A: fits that either failed to converge or returned an estimate on the edge of the search interval, out of 200 per cell.

Bias in estimated fishing mortality

Code 
summ_a <- res_a[conv == 0, .(
  median_F = median(F_hat),
  rel_bias = median(F_hat) / om$F_true - 1,
  mcse     = mcse_median(F_hat) / om$F_true
), by = .(case, X_true, mode)][order(X_true, mode)]

knitr::kable(summ_a, digits = 3,
             col.names = c("Case", "True RR", "Estimator",

Do the flag settings bracket the truth?

Code 
bracket_check <- function(dt, f_true) {
  id   <- setdiff(names(dt), c("mode", "F_hat", "conv"))
  keep <- dt[mode %in% c("flag0", "flag1")]

  # Keep only replicates where BOTH flag modes converged. Filtering per mode
  # and then reshaping silently produces NA and poisons the cell mean.
  ok   <- keep[, .(both = all(conv == 0) & .N == 2L), by = id][both == TRUE]
  keep <- merge(keep, ok[, ..id], by = id)

  w <- dcast(keep, stats::as.formula(paste(paste(id, collapse = " + "), "~ mode")),
             value.var = "F_hat")
  w[, `:=`(lo = pmin(flag0, flag1), hi = pmax(flag0, flag1))]
  w[, brackets := f_true >= lo & f_true <= hi]
  stopifnot(!anyNA(w$brackets))
  w[]
}

wide_a <- bracket_check(res_a[, .(rep, case, X_true, mode, F_hat, conv)], om$F_true)

knitr::kable(
  wide_a[, .(`flag1 (median)` = median(flag1),
             `flag0 (median)` = median(flag0),
             `true F`         = om$F_true,
             `% bracketing`   = 100 * mean(brackets)),
         by = .(case, X_true)][order(X_true)],
  digits = 3)

At the baseline configuration the two settings sit on the same side of the truth in both misspecified cases (0.0% bracketing). flag1 is uniformly the lower of the two, so the pair spans an interval — but that interval lies wholly above or wholly below the truth. Note that being the lower endpoint is not the same as being the closer one: in the true < assumed case flag1 is further from the truth than flag0, not less extreme.

The one case with non-zero bracketing is the case where the reporting rate is assumed correctly, at 46.5%. That is worth reading carefully, because it is not evidence that the pair works. When \(X\) is right, flag0 is unbiased, so it sits on the truth and Monte Carlo noise puts it above the truth roughly half the time. The “bracket” is really just flag0 landing on the answer, with flag1 some distance below it. A construct that only contains the truth when one of its two endpoints is already unbiased is not bounding anything.

Experiment B shows why the asymmetry between the two misspecified cases is structural rather than incidental.

Experiment B: mixing length and mixing-period availability

Two things the assessment configuration controls directly are added to the design:

  • Mixing length nmix \(\in \{2,3,4\}\) quarters — this is tag_flags(i,1), chosen by the analyst.
  • Availability during mixing \(\varphi \in \{0.5, 1.0, 2.0\}\) — tagged fish half as catchable as average, equally catchable, or twice as catchable. The last case represents concentrated effort around release sites and is not exotic for purse-seine tagging.

These are crossed with the same three reporting-rate scenarios, giving 27 cells. Note that \(\varphi\) is a property of the world, not a setting: no estimator is told its value, and only the forward parameterisations even have a parameter for it.

Runtime note: this design is 3 x 3 x 3 x 4 x n_rep_b model fits. Half of those are one-dimensional and cheap; the forward modes are the cost. Expect a few minutes. Drop n_rep_b to 20 for a quick pass; the medians get noisier — watch the MCSE column — but the patterns hold.

Code 
n_rep_b <- 60          # raise for smoother medians; runtime scales linearly

design_b <- CJ(nmix   = c(2L, 3L, 4L),
               phi    = c(0.5, 1.0, 2.0),
               X_true = scenarios$X_true,
               mode   = modes,
               rep    = seq_len(n_rep_b), sorted = FALSE) %>%
  merge(scenarios, by = "X_true")

# Seed from a group index rather than an arithmetic combination of the factor
# levels, which is collision-prone as soon as a level or the replicate count
# changes.
design_b[, cell := .GRP, by = .(nmix, phi, X_true)]

res_b <- design_b[, {
  set.seed(1000L * cell + rep)
  r <- simulate_returns(om, X_true, phi = phi, nmix = nmix)
  fit_one(r, om, mode = mode, nmix = nmix)
}, by = .(rep, cell, nmix, phi, X_true, case, mode)]

res_b[, `:=`(mode     = factor(mode, levels = modes),
             rel_bias = F_hat / om$F_true - 1)]

The survival floor engages in 0.0% of replicates across the 27-cell design. The Experiment B results can therefore be read as the floor-free case throughout, and Experiment C is where the floor becomes the story. Establishing this matters for how the two experiments are read against each other: the robustness result below is a floor-free result, and the Experiment C reversal is attributable to the floor rather than to any other difference between the designs.

The flag0 robustness result

One column of the design deserves separate attention: what happens when the reporting rate is assumed correctly, and only \(\varphi\) and nmix vary.

Code 
ggplot(summ_b[case == "true = assumed"],
       aes(factor(nmix), rel_bias, colour = mode, group = mode)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ phi, labeller = labeller(phi = function(x) paste0("phi = ", x))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal) +
  labs(x = "Mixing periods (nmix)", y = "Median relative bias in F-hat",
       colour = NULL)

flag0 is close to unbiased across every combination of \(\varphi\) and nmix, provided the reporting rate is right — the largest absolute median bias in the nine cells is 2.7%. This is not an accident and it is worth stating plainly, because it is the strongest argument for the default setting: the deterministic inversion solves for whatever mixing-period \(F\) reproduces the implied removal, so it never needs to know \(\varphi\). Misspecifying the availability of tagged fish during mixing — the very thing the mixing period exists to handle — costs flag0 nothing.

flag1 has no such protection. Its error is the recaptures it fails to remove, which is a fraction \((1 - X)\) of the true recaptures, accumulated over every mixing period. Both raising \(\varphi\) and lengthening nmix increase the number of recaptures during mixing, so both make it worse — sharply. At \(\varphi = 2\) and nmix = 4 the bias in \(F\) is -63%, which is a large upward error in biomass.

Does bracketing ever occur?

Code 
wide_b <- bracket_check(
  res_b[, .(rep, nmix, phi, X_true, case, mode, F_hat, conv)], om$F_true)

brk_b <- wide_b[, .(pct = 100 * mean(brackets),
                    width = median((hi - lo) / om$F_true)),
                by = .(nmix, phi, case)]

ggplot(brk_b, aes(factor(nmix), factor(phi), fill = pct)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f%%", pct)), size = 3.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ case) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#F1EFE8", high = "#7F77DD", limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "Mixing periods (nmix)", y = "phi", fill = "% bracketing")
Code 
ggplot(brk_b, aes(factor(nmix), width, colour = factor(phi), group = factor(phi))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ case) +
  labs(x = "Mixing periods (nmix)", y = "Interval width / true F",
       colour = "phi")

The heat map has a hard structural edge: bracketing never occurs anywhere in the true < assumed column (maximum 0%), at any \(\varphi\) or nmix. That is not sampling noise, and it follows from the arithmetic. Because \(X_{assumed} < 1\), the raised target \(R_t / X_{assumed}\) always exceeds \(R_t\), so flag0 always removes more tags than flag1 and therefore always returns the larger \(\hat{F}\). The interval is always \([\,\hat{F}_{\text{flag1}},\ \hat{F}_{\text{flag0}}\,]\), with flag0 as its upper end. Bracketing therefore requires \(\hat{F}_{\text{flag0}} \ge F_{true}\), and flag0 only sits above the truth when the true reporting rate is at or above what was assumed.

The pair is a one-sided construct. It can only ever bracket from below, and only when the assumed reporting rate errs low. If your concern is that the assumed reporting rate is too high, running both flag settings cannot bound the truth no matter what else is going on in the model — and no diagnostic internal to the pair will tell you which side you are on.

Within the two columns where bracketing does appear, it appears for different reasons:

  • true = assumed (38–57% throughout). The degenerate case described in Experiment A: flag0 is unbiased, so noise straddles the truth about half the time. The rate is flat across \(\varphi\) and nmix because it reflects Monte Carlo scatter, not a property of the configuration.
  • true > assumed (0% to 100%). Genuine two-sided coverage, arising where flag0 has blown up upward far enough that flag1’s own downward bias falls below the truth. This is two opposite-signed biases happening to cross. It appears in the following cells: phi = 1, nmix = 3 (5%); phi = 1, nmix = 4 (33%); phi = 2, nmix = 2 (32%); phi = 2, nmix = 3 (100%); phi = 2, nmix = 4 (100%) — that is, it needs high availability, and at \(\varphi = 1\) it needs a long mixing period as well.

Interval width tracks that story. Where bracketing is genuine, the interval is enormous: at \(\varphi = 2\) and nmix = 4 it spans roughly 1.8 times the true \(F\). An interval that contains the truth but is nearly twice as wide as the quantity being estimated is not usable as an uncertainty statement. Where bracketing is degenerate (true = assumed), the interval is tight — 0.1 to 0.6 times \(F\) — but that tightness is meaningless, because it is anchored by an endpoint that happens to be unbiased for reasons the analyst cannot verify from inside the model.

The survival-floor condition

At extreme availability the raised target \(R_t / X_{assumed}\) can drive the tagged population below the survival floor, which is the condition that triggers the posfun rescaling in do_newton_raphson_for_tags().

It is worth being precise about the threshold, because the obvious statement of it is not the one the code implements. Reported returns can never exceed true recaptures, \(R_t \le C_t\), so exhaustion of the tagged population, \(R_t / X_{assumed} > N_t\), requires \(C_t / N_t > X_{assumed}\). But MULTIFAN-CL does not wait for exhaustion: it floors survival at \(\tau = 0.22\) (the age_flags(118)/(119) defaults). The condition that actually engages the floor is therefore

\[\frac{R_t}{X_{assumed}} > (1 - \tau)\, N_t \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{C_t}{N_t} > (1 - \tau)\, X_{assumed},\]

which at the default \(\tau\) is a catch fraction of about 0.78 times the assumed reporting rate — roughly a fifth easier to reach than the exhaustion version. At \(X_{assumed} = 0.5\) that is 0.390; at \(X_{assumed} = 0.2\) it is 0.156, which ordinary fishing mortalities reach without anything unusual happening.

This is the formal version of the trip-level argument: a trip taking a large part of a release group and reporting all of it engages the floor, and the lower the assumed reporting rate the smaller that part needs to be. The manual’s warning is therefore less about reporting rates being uncertain than about their being low.

Code 
floor_grid <- CJ(nmix = c(2L, 3L, 4L), phi = c(0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0),
                 rep = seq_len(150), sorted = FALSE)
floor_grid[, cell := .GRP, by = .(nmix, phi)]

floor_res <- floor_grid[, {
  set.seed(1000L * cell + rep)
  r <- simulate_returns(om, X_true = 0.65, phi = phi, nmix = nmix)
  .(hits = floor_check_one(r, om, nmix))
}, by = .(rep, cell, nmix, phi)]

ggplot(floor_res[, .(pct = 100 * mean(hits > 0)), by = .(nmix, phi)],
       aes(factor(nmix), factor(phi), fill = pct)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f%%", pct)), size = 3.2) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#F1EFE8", high = "#D85A30", limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "Mixing periods (nmix)", y = "phi", fill = "% floored")

Within the range of \(\varphi\) used in the main design (\(\varphi \le 2\)) the floor never engages. Beyond it, the floor is reached in more than half of replicates in the following cells: phi = 4 with nmix = 3, phi = 4 with nmix = 4.

The mechanism is worth noting because it is not obvious from the catch fraction alone: within a mixing period \(C_t/N_t\) is constant, but the estimator’s tagged population declines faster than the simulator’s whenever the target is raised too far, so the ratio the floor tests against grows with each mixing period. That is why longer mixing periods trigger the floor at a given \(\varphi\) when short ones do not.

Two things are worth checking in any real configuration: whether that threshold is being reached for any release group, and whether age_flags(117) < 0, in which case the penalty weight is zero and the rescaling happens with no trace at all in the objective function.

A reader arriving here from Experiment C will see engagement rates that look incompatible with this sweep, and they are not. This sweep uses Experiment A/B’s observation model: one release cohort of 10,000 tags with deterministic Baranov recaptures, in which the realised catch fraction barely departs from its expectation, so only extreme availability pushes it over the threshold. Experiment C uses several small groups with stochastic recaptures and clumped reporting, where the same expected catch fraction produces realisations well into the tail. The threshold is the same; what differs is how far the realisations stray from it, and that is a property of release-group size and the reporting process, not of the floor.

Recovery of the availability multiplier

Code 
phi_res <- res_b[mode %in% c("forward", "forward_X") & conv == 0 &
                   case == "true > assumed",
                 .(nmix, phi, mode, phi_hat)]

ggplot(phi_res, aes(factor(nmix), phi_hat, fill = mode)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.4, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = phi), linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~ phi, scales = "free_y",
             labeller = labeller(phi = function(x) paste0("true phi = ", x))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal) +
  labs(x = "Mixing periods (nmix)", y = expression(hat(varphi)), fill = NULL)

Note that this figure conditions on one reporting-rate scenario (true > assumed); the panels are values of \(\varphi\), not reporting-rate cases.

forward_X recovers \(\varphi\) accurately at all three values, including \(\varphi > 1\), and its accuracy is stable across mixing lengths — the largest median error across the nine (nmix, \(\varphi\)) combinations is 3%.

forward does not, and the pattern is diagnostic. With \(X\) pinned at the wrong value, \(\hat{\varphi}\) is pulled toward 1 and the pull strengthens as the mixing period lengthens: at true \(\varphi = 2\) the median falls from 1.66 at nmix = 2 to 1.43 at nmix = 4. The availability multiplier is absorbing the reporting-rate error, and a longer mixing period gives it more periods over which to do so. This is worth knowing before proposing \(\varphi\) to the developers: estimating it is only useful if the reporting rate is also free to move, otherwise \(\varphi\) becomes a sponge for reporting-rate misspecification rather than an estimate of availability.

Consistency with Experiment A

Experiment A’s configuration (nmix = 2, \(\varphi = 0.5\)) is one cell of Experiment B, fitted to independently drawn data. The two should agree to within Monte Carlo error, and checking that they do is the cheapest available test that the shared machinery is behaving.

  by = c("case", "mode"))
ab[, `:=`(diff = A - B, joint_mcse = sqrt(A_mcse^2 + B_mcse^2))]

Experiment C: a realistic reporting process and the survival-floor failure mode

Experiments A and B use a deliberately clean observation model: a single release group of 10,000 tags, deterministic Baranov recaptures, and independent Poisson reporting. That model cannot produce the failure the MULTIFAN-CL manual warns about, because with 10,000 tags and independent reporting the realised recapture fraction never strays far from its expectation.

Three ingredients are missing, and all three are properties of real tagging data:

  1. Release groups are small. Hundreds, not tens of thousands, once split by region and quarter.
  2. Recaptures are stochastic, not a deterministic Baranov quantity.
  3. Reporting is clumped at the trip level. Whether a tag is reported depends largely on whether that trip reports, so returns arrive in batches. The reporting rate is an average over trips, but the realisation for any one release group is close to all-or-nothing when few trips are involved.

This section adds all three and asks when the default setting actually breaks. The mixing-period machinery is unchanged from Experiments A and B — it is the same mix_step — so any difference in behaviour is attributable to the observation model and to release-group size, not to a different cap.

Machinery

Code 
# ---- stochastic Baranov + clumped trip-level reporting ---------------------
# Each fish is caught, dies naturally, or survives (multinomial), so the
# population dynamics stay consistent with the Baranov equation the estimator
# assumes. Setting stochastic = FALSE and trip_size = 1 recovers the
# Experiment A/B observation model.
#
# `expected = TRUE` is a third path, added for the sufficiency test in
# Experiment D: it substitutes the expectation at BOTH stages, so neither the
# population dynamics nor the reporting step carries any Monte Carlo noise, and
# it works in doubles throughout because rounding the catch to whole fish would
# show up in the third decimal of a structural bias. `stochastic = FALSE` alone
# de-randomises only the dynamics -- the reporting step stays binomial -- which
# is why a separate argument is needed rather than an overload.
#
# The realised number of reporting trips per period is attached as an
# attribute, because it is the quantity that actually drives the clumping and
# it is not recoverable from trip_size alone.
simulate_group <- function(p, N0, X_g, phi, nmix,
                           trip_size = 1, stochastic = TRUE,
                           expected = FALSE) {
  if (expected && stochastic)
    stop("`expected` and `stochastic` are mutually exclusive; ",
         "set stochastic = FALSE when asking for expected returns.")
  if (expected && trip_size > 1)
    stop("`expected` is only defined for un-clumped reporting (trip_size = 1).")

  n <- if (expected) as.numeric(N0) else as.integer(N0)
  r <- numeric(p$Tmax)
  ktrips <- rep(NA_integer_, p$Tmax)

  for (t in seq_len(p$Tmax)) {
    f_t <- p$F_true * if (t <= nmix) phi else 1
    z   <- f_t + p$M
    s   <- exp(-z)
    u   <- f_t / z * (1 - s)             # caught
    v   <- p$M  / z * (1 - s)            # natural death

    if (stochastic) {
      draw <- rmultinom(1, n, c(u, v, s))
      catch <- draw[1]; surv <- draw[3]
    } else if (expected) {
      catch <- u * n; surv <- s * n
    } else {
      catch <- as.integer(round(u * n)); surv <- as.integer(round(s * n))
    }

    if (expected) {
      r[t] <- X_g * catch
      ktrips[t] <- NA_integer_
    } else if (catch > 0) {
      if (trip_size <= 1) {
        r[t] <- rbinom(1, catch, X_g)
        ktrips[t] <- catch
      } else {
        k     <- max(round(catch / trip_size), 1)
        alloc <- rmultinom(1, catch, rep(1 / k, k))
        r[t]  <- sum(alloc[runif(k) < X_g])
        ktrips[t] <- k
      }
    }
    n <- surv
  }
  attr(r, "ktrips") <- ktrips
  r
}

# ---- multi-group objective, shared F ---------------------------------------
# `kernel = TRUE` replaces dpois() with the Poisson kernel mu - r*log(mu). The
# discarded term, lgamma(r + 1), does not depend on any parameter, so the
# argmin is unchanged. It is needed because expected returns are not integers
# and dpois() returns zero density (and a warning) for non-integer x, which
# would make the deterministic fits in Experiment D fail rather than converge.
nll_multi <- function(par, groups, p, mode, nmix, prior_sd = 0.4,
                      kernel = FALSE) {
  f_pop <- exp(par[1])
  phi   <- if (mode %in% c("forward", "forward_X")) exp(par[2]) else 1
  x     <- if (mode == "forward_X") plogis(par[3]) else p$X_assumed

  nll <- 0
  for (g in seq_along(groups)) {
    r <- groups[[g]]$returns
    n <- groups[[g]]$N0

    for (t in seq_len(p$Tmax)) {
      premix <- t <= nmix

      if (premix && mode %in% c("flag0", "flag1")) {
        st  <- mix_step(r[t], n, p, mode)
        f_t <- st$f
        nll <- nll + PENWT * st$pen
      } else {
        f_t <- if (premix) f_pop * phi else f_pop
        mu  <- x * baranov(f_t, n, p$M) + 1e-10
        nll <- nll + if (kernel) mu - r[t] * log(mu)
                     else -dpois(r[t], mu, log = TRUE)
      }
      n <- n * exp(-(f_t + p$M))
    }
  }

  if (mode == "forward_X") {
    nll <- nll + 0.5 * ((log(x) - log(p$X_assumed)) / prior_sd)^2
  }
  nll
}

fit_multi <- function(groups, p, mode, nmix, interval = LOGF_INT,
                      kernel = FALSE) {
  mode <- as.character(mode)[1L]

  if (mode %in% c("flag0", "flag1")) {
    opt <- stats::optimize(
      function(lf) nll_multi(c(lf, 0, 0), groups, p, mode, nmix,
                             kernel = kernel),
      interval = interval, tol = 1e-10)
    return(data.table(F_hat = exp(opt$minimum), phi_hat = NA_real_,
                      X_hat = p$X_assumed, conv = 0L,
                      at_bound = at_bound_lf(opt$minimum, interval)))
  }

  opt <- stats::optim(
    par = c(log(0.10), 0, qlogis(p$X_assumed)),
    fn  = function(par) nll_multi(par, groups, p, mode, nmix,
                                  kernel = kernel),
    method = "Nelder-Mead",
    control = list(maxit = 4000, reltol = 1e-11))

  data.table(F_hat    = exp(opt$par[1]),
             phi_hat  = exp(opt$par[2]),
             X_hat    = if (mode == "forward_X") plogis(opt$par[3]) else p$X_assumed,
             conv     = opt$convergence,
             at_bound = FALSE)
}

# ---- diagnostic: how often, and how widely, does the floor engage? ---------
# Uses the same mix_step as the estimator, so the two advance the tagged
# population identically. If they were allowed to diverge, the floor frequency
# reported here would not be the one the estimator experienced.
floor_check <- function(groups, p, nmix) {
  hits <- 0L; tot <- 0L
  for (g in seq_along(groups)) {
    r <- groups[[g]]$returns; n <- groups[[g]]$N0
    for (t in seq_len(nmix)) {
      st <- mix_step(r[t], n, p, "flag0")
      if (st$floored) hits <- hits + 1L
      tot <- tot + 1L
      n <- n * exp(-(st$f + p$M))
    }
  }
  list(any = hits > 0L, hits = hits, frac = hits / tot)
}

Design

Eight release groups of 500 tags each, sharing one fishing mortality, with a mixing period of nmix = 3 quarters and availability \(\varphi \in \{1, 2\}\). The mixing length is fixed here — Experiment B is the experiment that varies it — which matters when reading Experiment C against Experiment B’s claim of robustness across nmix.

The assumed reporting rate becomes a factor: it is the axis the survival-floor condition depends on, and it is the quantity under dispute in the current assessment. Trip size is expressed as a percentage of the release group, so 25% means a trip large enough to take a quarter of the group.

Runtime note: this design carries all four estimators. Two of them are one-dimensional, so the cost is dominated by the two forward modes and is lower than the estimator count suggests.

Group-specific reporting rates are drawn on the logit scale and recentred there. Drawing them on the natural scale would require clamping away from zero, which at \(X_{assumed} = 0.2\) truncates enough of the distribution to induce a small upward bias in the realised mean rate — an artefact of the sampling scheme that would be indistinguishable from an estimator property. The cost of working on the logit scale is that the arithmetic mean of the realised rates is correct only to within a Jensen term; that term is reported below so its size is visible rather than assumed.

Code 
n_rep_c    <- 30           # raise for smoother medians
G          <- 8            # release groups
N0_g       <- 500          # tags per group
rr_sd_lgt  <- 0.45         # between-group sd of logit(reporting rate)
NMIX_C     <- 3L           # mixing periods, fixed for this experiment

modes_c <- c("flag0", "flag1", "forward", "forward_X")

design_c <- CJ(X_assumed = c(0.20, 0.35, 0.50),
               trip_pct  = c(0.01, 0.10, 0.25),
               phi       = c(1.0, 2.0),
               mode      = modes_c,
               rep       = seq_len(n_rep_c), sorted = FALSE)

# `cell` deliberately excludes `mode`, so all four estimators see the same
# simulated dataset within a replicate and the comparison stays paired.
design_c[, cell := .GRP, by = .(X_assumed, trip_pct, phi)]

make_groups <- function(p, phi, nmix, trip_pct, rr_sd_logit) {
  lx <- rnorm(G, qlogis(p$X_assumed), rr_sd_logit)
  lx <- lx - mean(lx) + qlogis(p$X_assumed)   # exact on the logit scale
  xs <- plogis(lx)
  gs <- lapply(seq_len(G), function(g)
    list(N0 = N0_g,
         X_g = xs[g],
         returns = simulate_group(p, N0_g, xs[g], phi, nmix,
                                  trip_size = max(trip_pct * N0_g, 1),
                                  stochastic = TRUE)))
  gs
}

res_c <- design_c[, {
  p <- modifyList(om, list(X_assumed = X_assumed))
  set.seed(1000L * cell + rep)
  gs  <- make_groups(p, phi, NMIX_C, trip_pct, rr_sd_lgt)
  fit <- fit_multi(gs, p, mode = mode, nmix = NMIX_C)
  fl  <- floor_check(gs, p, NMIX_C)
  cbind(fit,
        floored     = fl$any,
        floor_frac  = fl$frac,
        mean_X      = mean(vapply(gs, `[[`, numeric(1), "X_g")),
        min_ktrips  = min(vapply(gs, function(g) {
                          kt <- attr(g$returns, "ktrips")[seq_len(NMIX_C)]
                          kt <- kt[!is.na(kt)]
                          if (!length(kt)) NA_real_ else as.numeric(min(kt))
                        }, numeric(1)), na.rm = TRUE))
}, by = .(rep, cell, X_assumed, trip_pct, phi, mode)]

The trip table is worth pausing on. At trip_pct = 0.1 and \(\varphi = 1\) the median release group has as few as 1 reporting trip in its worst mixing period. “A trip takes a quarter of the group” understates what is happening at that corner of the design: the period’s entire catch is close to a single all-or-nothing reporting decision. That is the cell driving the top-right of the map below, and it should be read as the extreme end of the clumping axis rather than as a typical fishery.

How often does the floor engage?

Three factors drive the failure, and none of them is a reporting-rate error.

The assumed reporting rate is the strongest. At \(X_{assumed} = 0.5\) with \(\varphi = 1\) the floor engages in 0% of replicates; at \(X_{assumed} = 0.2\) with \(\varphi = 2\) it is 57–100%. This follows directly from the condition above: a lower assumed rate sets a lower bar for the realised catch fraction to clear.

Availability during mixing matters nearly as much. Moving from \(\varphi = 1\) to \(\varphi = 2\) raises the \(X_{assumed} = 0.5\) row from 0% to 3–67%. More recaptures during mixing means more opportunity for one of them to be an extreme realisation. This is why the summary qualifies the moderate-reporting-rate case: a moderate assumed rate is not on its own a guarantee that the floor is inactive.

Trip size matters, but it is the weakest of the three. Coarse reporting makes the failure more frequent — at \(X_{assumed} = 0.2\), \(\varphi = 1\) it rises from 17% to 67% across the trip-size range — but fine-grained reporting does not protect you when the other two factors are adverse: at \(X_{assumed} = 0.2\) and \(\varphi = 2\), trips taking just 1% of a release group still trigger it in 57% of replicates.

This is the mechanism behind the manual’s recommendation, and it is governed mainly by the assumed reporting rate. An assessment that revises its tag-seeding estimates downward moves itself into the regime where the default breaks, without changing anything else about the model.

The headline from Experiment B does not survive intact, and the pattern divides cleanly along the floor frequency mapped above.

Where the floor rarely engages, the cost is precision. At \(X_{assumed} = 0.5\) with \(\varphi = 1\), flag0’s median bias stays within 4%, consistent with Experiment B. But its interquartile range widens from 0.18 to 0.43 as trip size coarsens. Individual replicates swing in both directions, because a single release group whose trips happened to report can drive the raised removal, and hence the whole estimate of \(F\), a long way.

Where the floor routinely engages, the cost is accuracy, and it runs downward. At \(X_{assumed} = 0.2\) with \(\varphi = 2\), flag0’s median bias ranges over -36% to +11%: +11% at trip size 1%, -28% at trip size 10%, -36% at trip size 25%. Between the least- and most-clumped cells the median moves by -47% against a joint Monte Carlo standard error of 10.8%, so that shift is resolved by this design. Taken step by step, 1 of the 2 successive differences is resolved against its own Monte Carlo error, so the step-by-step ordering of the cells is not a result of this design, and only the movement between its ends should be read as one. The cell on the positive side is the one where the floor bites least (4% of group-periods floored); the cell where it bites hardest (16%) is on the negative side. Note that even the mildest of the three floors in 57% of replicates, so engagement frequency alone does not locate the sign change. Floor severity and clumping rise together across this row, so the design cannot separate them – what it shows is that the sign turns over as the floor takes hold. The mechanism deserves to be stated explicitly: once posfun caps the removal, flag0 can no longer take out the number of tags its own rule demands, so it under-removes — which is precisely flag1’s failure mode. Under floor engagement the default degenerates toward the alternative it is supposed to improve on, and the bias it contributes runs negative, meaning biomass biased upward.

This is the most important qualification to the Experiment B result. The unbiasedness of flag0 is conditional not only on the reporting rate being right, but on the survival floor not engaging — and the second condition is easiest to violate exactly when assumed reporting rates are low.

flag1 behaves as Experiment D predicts throughout: median bias in -68% to -27%, driven by \(\varphi\) rather than by trip size, and consistently the most precise of the estimators (interquartile ranges of 0.09 to 0.54). Precisely wrong is still wrong, but flag1’s error is at least predictable in a way flag0’s is not.

forward_X needs a caveat of its own here. Its accuracy in Experiments A and B does not carry over to this small-sample, multi-group setting: medians range over -46% to +35%, and interquartile ranges reach 1.34. It is the widest of the estimators in 89% of the 18 cells. With eight groups of 500 tags there is not enough information to estimate the reporting rate, the availability multiplier and \(F\) simultaneously. The likelihood-based treatment is structurally correct but it is not free: it needs data to support the extra parameters, and a fragmented tagging programme may not supply them.

Does the mixing-channel decomposition survive?

forward is included here for the same reason it exists in Experiments A and B: it handles the mixing period correctly while keeping \(X\) fixed at the assumed value, so the flag0–forward gap isolates what the mixing treatment contributes beyond the reporting-rate channel. Experiment C is the experiment that overturns the other Experiment B headlines, so the decomposition should not be assumed to carry over.

Code

       aes(factor(100 * trip_pct), med, colour = mode, group = mode)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  facet_grid(X_assumed ~ phi,
             labeller = labeller(phi = function(x) paste0("phi = ", x),
                                 X_assumed = function(x) paste0("X = ", x))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal) +
  labs(x = "Trip size (% of release group)", y = "Median relative bias in F-hat",
       colour = NULL)

Note that in this experiment the reporting rate is correct on average, so forward is not carrying a reporting-rate error in the way it does in Experiments A and B; the gap here isolates the deterministic inversion against a correctly specified alternative rather than decomposing a misspecification. Where the floor is inactive (\(X_{assumed} = 0.5\), \(\varphi = 1\)) the two agree to within 1%. Where it is active the gap widens to -38% to +5%, with the largest single gap (-38%) at \(X_{assumed} = 0.2\), \(\varphi = 2\), trip size 25%. The deterministic treatment is therefore a second-order channel exactly where the floor is inactive and a first-order one where it is not — the same boundary that governs everything else in this experiment.

Experiment D: the mixing-period recapture fraction

Experiment B varied \(\varphi\) and nmix separately, which is how an analyst encounters them — one is a property of the fishery, the other a configuration choice. But for flag1 they are not two effects. Both act only by changing how many tags are recaptured while the mixing rule is in force.

Define

\[\psi = \frac{1}{N_0}\sum_{t \le n_{mix}} C_t,\]

the expected fraction of a release group recaptured during the mixing period. This is directly computable from a real .tag file given tag_flags(i,1), which makes it the useful axis: an analyst can measure \(\psi\) for their own data and read off the expected bias.

Why \(\psi\) should govern the flag1 bias

flag1 removes \(R_t\) where it should remove \(C_t\), so in expectation it under-removes by \((1 - X)\,C_t\) each mixing period, and \((1-X)\,\psi N_0\) in total. The surviving tagged cohort entering the informative periods is therefore too large by that amount. Predicted recaptures scale with the cohort, so to match the observed post-mixing returns the model compensates with a smaller \(F\):

\[\frac{\hat{F}}{F} \;\approx\; \frac{N_{post}}{N_{post} + (1-X)\,\psi N_0}, \qquad N_{post} = N_0\,e^{-(\varphi F + M)\,n_{mix}}.\]

Note carefully what this does and does not predict. The bias depends on \(\varphi\) and nmix only through \(\psi\) and \(N_{post}\) — but \(N_{post}\) carries an nmix dependence of its own, over and above the one that runs through \(\psi\). Two configurations with different \(\varphi\) and nmix but the same \(\psi\) are therefore predicted to be close, not identical, and the one with the longer mixing period is predicted to be the worse of the two: it reaches the same recapture fraction with a smaller surviving cohort to carry the un-removed tags. Whether that separation is large enough to matter for an assessment is a quantitative question, and it is the one the sufficiency test below is built to answer.

Code 
psi_of <- function(p, phi, nmix) {
  n <- p$N0; tot <- 0
  for (t in seq_len(nmix)) {
    tot <- tot + baranov(p$F_true * phi, n, p$M)
    n   <- n * exp(-(p$F_true * phi + p$M))
  }
  tot / p$N0
}

bias_pred <- function(p, phi, nmix, X) {
  psi   <- psi_of(p, phi, nmix)
  npost <- p$N0 * exp(-(p$F_true * phi + p$M) * nmix)
  under <- (1 - X) * psi * p$N0
  -under / (npost + under)
}

# psi_of() is monotone increasing in phi at fixed nmix, so it can be inverted
# for a target recapture fraction. This is what turns psi from an outcome of
# the design into a controlled variable, and it is the whole basis of the
# sufficiency test below: without it, no two cells share a psi exactly.
phi_for_psi <- function(target, nmix, p = om, phi_max = 20) {
  if (psi_of(p, phi_max, nmix) < target) return(NA_real_)
  uniroot(function(ph) psi_of(p, ph, nmix) - target,
          interval = c(1e-8, phi_max), tol = 1e-10)$root
}

# The loop in psi_of() and the closed form below are the same quantity: summing
# Baranov catch over a geometrically declining cohort telescopes to
# (phi*F/Z)(1 - exp(-nmix*Z)). Asserting it keeps the two from drifting if
# either is edited, and documents where the closed form comes from -- it is the
# expression an analyst needs to compute expected psi for a configuration they
# have not run.
psi_closed <- function(p, phi, nmix) {
  z <- p$F_true * phi + p$M
  (p$F_true * phi / z) * (1 - exp(-nmix * z))
}
stopifnot(all(abs(mapply(function(ph, nm) psi_of(om, ph, nm) -
                           psi_closed(om, ph, nm),
                         c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3),
                         c(2L, 3L, 4L, 2L, 3L))) < 1e-12))

Simulation

Reporting is left un-clumped here so that \(\psi\) is isolated from the dispersion effects of Experiment C. Four release groups of 2,000 tags, correct reporting rate throughout, so the only thing varying is how much of each group is recaptured before the mixing rule releases its grip.

Code 
n_rep_d <- 40
N0_d    <- 2000
G_d     <- 4

design_d <- CJ(phi  = c(0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0),
               nmix = c(2L, 3L, 4L),
               mode = c("flag0", "flag1"),
               rep  = seq_len(n_rep_d), sorted = FALSE)
design_d[, cell := .GRP, by = .(phi, nmix)]

res_d <- design_d[, {
  set.seed(1000L * cell + rep)
  gs <- lapply(seq_len(G_d), function(g)
    list(N0 = N0_d,
         returns = simulate_group(om, N0_d, om$X_assumed, phi, nmix,
                                  trip_size = 1, stochastic = TRUE)))
  fit_multi(gs, om, mode = mode, nmix = nmix)
}, by = .(rep, cell, phi, nmix, mode)]

res_d[, `:=`(mode = factor(mode, levels = c("flag0", "flag1")),
             rel_bias = F_hat / om$F_true - 1)]

summ_d <- res_d[conv == 0, .(bias = median(rel_bias),
                             mcse = mcse_median(F_hat) / om$F_true),
                by = .(phi, nmix, mode)]
summ_d[, psi  := psi_of(om, phi, nmix), by = .(phi, nmix)]
summ_d[, pred := bias_pred(om, phi, nmix, om$X_assumed), by = .(phi, nmix)]

Is \(\psi\) sufficient?

The design above crosses \(\varphi\) and nmix and reports whatever \(\psi\) falls out, so no two cells share a \(\psi\) exactly and the collapse onto a single curve can only be judged by eye against the fitted line. The question the prediction actually raises — whether two configurations with the same \(\psi\) behave the same — needs a design in which \(\psi\) is controlled rather than observed.

Inverting psi_of() supplies one. Solving for the \(\varphi\) that delivers a target \(\psi\) at each mixing length puts the cells on a common \(\psi\) grid, and fitting to expected rather than simulated returns removes the Monte Carlo noise entirely, so any separation between mixing lengths at the same \(\psi\) is structural rather than scatter. No Monte Carlo standard errors are reported in this subsection because there is no Monte Carlo.

Code 
PSI_TARGETS <- c(0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50)

calib <- CJ(psi_t = PSI_TARGETS, nmix = 2:4)
calib[, phi := mapply(phi_for_psi, psi_t, nmix)]
calib <- calib[is.finite(phi)]

knitr::kable(dcast(calib, psi_t ~ nmix, value.var = "phi"), digits = 2,
             col.names = c("psi", "nmix = 2", "nmix = 3", "nmix = 4"),
             caption = paste0(
               "Availability multiplier required to reach each target ",
               "recapture fraction, by mixing length."))

Reaching a high \(\psi\) over a short mixing period requires a large availability multiplier; reaching the same \(\psi\) over four periods requires much less. Code 
grid_suff <- CJ(psi_t = PSI_TARGETS, nmix = 2:4,
                mode = c("flag0", "flag1"), sorted = FALSE)
grid_suff <- merge(grid_suff, calib, by = c("psi_t", "nmix"))

res_suff <- grid_suff[, {
  # One release group, expected returns, correct reporting rate. The Poisson
  # kernel rather than dpois(), because expected returns are not integers.
  g <- list(list(N0      = om$N0,
                 returns = simulate_group(om, om$N0, om$X_assumed, phi, nmix,
                                          trip_size = 1, stochastic = FALSE,
                                          expected = TRUE)))
  cbind(fit_multi(g, om, mode = mode, nmix = nmix, kernel = TRUE),
        floored = floor_check(g, om, nmix)$any)
}, by = .(psi_t, nmix, phi, mode)]

res_suff[, `:=`(rel_bias = F_hat / om$F_true - 1,
                psi      = mapply(function(ph, nm) psi_of(om, ph, nm),
                                  phi, nmix))]
res_suff[, pred := mapply(function(ph, nm) bias_pred(om, ph, nm, om$X_assumed),
                          phi, nmix)]

# The inversion should be exact, and nothing here should be sitting on a search
# bound or against the survival floor -- if either happens the numbers below
# describe the machinery rather than the estimator.
stopifnot(max(abs(res_suff$psi - res_suff$psi_t)) < 1e-8,
          !any(res_suff$at_bound))

\(\psi\) is close to sufficient, but it is not sufficient. At every target the ordering the theory predicts is present — a longer mixing period carries the worse bias at the same recapture fraction — and the separation widens as \(\psi\) does, from 0.9% at \(\psi = 0.05\) to 9.1% at \(\psi = 0.50\). Against a bias of -59.9% in that worst cell, a spread of that size is second order but not negligible: an analyst reading a single number off a \(\psi\) curve is making an error of roughly 15% of the quantity they are estimating, in a known direction.

That the separation exists is not a failure of the theory in Section 6.1 — the predictor carries the same nmix dependence through \(N_{post}\) and reproduces the ordering, giving a spread of 15.6% at the top of the grid against the fitted 9.1%. The approximation overstates the effect while getting its sign and ordering right. What fails is the looser statement, easy to make from the fitted curve alone, that the bias is a function of \(\psi\) simpliciter. It is a function of \(\psi\) and the mixing length, with the second term small.

flag0 is flat across the whole grid, as it must be: with expected returns and a correct reporting rate its inversion is exact. Its largest absolute deviation anywhere in the design is 0.0000%, which is the optimiser’s tolerance rather than a property of the estimator, and it is worth contrasting with the 7.3% residual in the Monte Carlo design above: that residual is sampling scatter, not structure, and this is the run that demonstrates it. The survival floor did not engage anywhere in this design, so the flag0 row is a clean benchmark and the flag1 numbers are attributable to the mixing-period treatment alone.

Reading this for a real assessment

The near-collapse onto a single curve is the practical result. flag1’s bias is not a property of the mixing-period length or of tag availability separately — it is largely a function of the recapture fraction those two things produce, and that fraction is measurable. For a real release group:

  1. Take tag_flags(i,1) for that group and sum the reported returns within that many periods of release.
  2. Raise by the assumed reporting rate and divide by the number released: \(\hat\psi_i \approx (1/X)\sum_{t \le \texttt{tag\_flags}(i,1)} R_{it} / N_i\). The .tag file records returns, not recaptures, so omitting the \(1/X\) returns \(X\psi\) — at a reporting rate near 0.5, half the true fraction.
  3. Read the expected downward bias in \(F\) off the curve, or evaluate \(-(1-X)\psi N_0 / (N_{post} + (1-X)\psi N_0)\) directly. Where the mixing period is long, take the pessimistic end of the range at that \(\psi\).

Two caveats travel with \(\hat\psi\). The raising uses the same assumed reporting rate whose correctness is in question, so \(\hat\psi\) inherits that error — and inherits it in the unhelpful direction, since a reporting rate that is too high understates \(\psi\) and therefore understates the bias. And a release-group-weighted mean aggregates over groups whose mixing lengths and availabilities differ, whereas the figures here apply a single value to a single cohort.

At \(\psi = 0.05\) the bias is -4.8% to -3.9% and arguably tolerable. By \(\psi = 0.3\) it is -33.4% to -27.7%, and by \(\psi = 0.50\) it reaches -59.9% to -50.9%. Whether tag_flags(i,2) = 1 is defensible for a given assessment is therefore an empirical question about that assessment’s tag data, not a general one — and it is a question the assessment team can answer in an afternoon.

flag0 is far flatter across the same range, but it is not exactly zero: its largest absolute median bias is -7% at \(\psi = 0.64\), and 1 of the 15 cells sits more than two Monte Carlo standard errors from zero. That single exception carries a negative sign and sits at the high-\(\psi\) end of the design. Whether that residual is Monte Carlo scatter or a real small-sample property of inverting a noisy target is what Experiment E asks. Note the direction the theory predicts: inverting a noisy target is convex in the target, so the mechanism, if present, biases \(F\) upward at small samples.

Experiment E: release-group size and the noisy-inversion bias

The flag0 residuals at high \(\psi\) have a candidate explanation. The estimator inverts an observed quantity: it solves for the \(F\) that removes \(R_t / X_{assumed}\) tags. That inversion is a convex function of the target over the relevant range, so by Jensen’s inequality the expectation of the solved \(F\) exceeds the \(F\) that would be solved from the expected target. The size of the gap grows with the noise-to-signal ratio of \(R_t\), which falls with release-group size.

If that is the mechanism, flag0’s bias should decline systematically as \(N_0\) rises, holding \(\psi\) fixed. It would matter if it did: it would be a third condition on the default’s unbiasedness — adequate release-group size — independent of both the reporting rate and the survival floor, and small release groups are the realistic case once releases are split by region and quarter.

Three design points are worth stating before the result, because each of them determines whether the experiment can detect the effect it is looking for and whether the number it reports means what it appears to mean.

The statistic has to be tail-aware, and the mean alone is not enough. Jensen’s inequality is a statement about \(E[\hat{F}]\), so the median — close to invariant under the monotone convexity being hypothesised — tests the mechanism with an instrument largely blind to it. But the mean has a problem of its own here. The solved \(F\) is unbounded above in principle and bounded in practice only by the search interval, so if the effect is carried by a handful of extreme replicates, the mean is partly a report on where the interval was placed. Three statistics are therefore reported together: the frequency of gross overshoot (the proportion of replicates returning \(\hat{F}\) more than 5\(\times\) the truth), which is the primary statistic because it is a bounded frequency and insensitive to the interval as long as the ceiling sits well above the threshold; the mean, which is what the convexity argument speaks to; and the median, for comparability with the rest of this document.

The whole design is run at two search intervals. Every cell is fitted twice, once over the interval used everywhere else in this document and once over a much wider one. If the reported effect is a property of the estimator, the two runs agree. If it is a property of the ceiling, they do not, and the mean is then not a quantity worth quoting. This check is reported before the verdict, not after it.

One release group, not four. fit_multi pools groups into a single objective, so four groups over four mixing periods averages sixteen independent noisy inversions before \(\hat{F}\) is formed. That averaging is exactly what the large-sample argument says washes the bias out, so pooling suppresses the quantity of interest. Experiment E therefore uses a single group, which maximises the noise-to-signal ratio available at a given \(N_0\).

Recapture fraction is held high — \(\psi = 0.52\), toward the upper end of the Experiment D range — because that is where the Experiment D residuals appeared. Total tags vary with group size, which affects the precision of the estimates but not their expectation; the MCSE columns are what to read against.

Runtime note: fitting at two intervals doubles this design, and the replicate count is set high because a tail frequency needs more replicates than a mean does. Every fit is still one-dimensional, so this remains among the cheaper of the five experiments; drop n_rep_e for a quick pass, but check the guard margin reported at the end of the section before trusting the verdict.

Code 
# A tail frequency is a much lower-powered statistic than a mean, so this
# experiment needs more replicates than a median-based one would. At the tail
# mass seen here, 200 replicates leaves the difference between the smallest and
# largest group sizes barely separable from its own Monte Carlo error.
n_rep_e <- 400
PHI_E   <- 2.0
NMIX_E  <- 4L
G_e     <- 1          # one group: pooling averages away the effect being tested

# The same simulated data are fitted over both intervals, so the two runs are
# paired and any difference is attributable to the ceiling alone.
intervals_e <- list(default = LOGF_INT, wide = LOGF_INT_WIDE)

design_e <- CJ(N0_e     = c(125, 250, 500, 2000, 10000),
               interval = names(intervals_e),
               rep      = seq_len(n_rep_e), sorted = FALSE)
design_e[, cell := .GRP, by = .(N0_e)]

res_e <- design_e[, {
  set.seed(1000L * cell + rep)
  gs <- lapply(seq_len(G_e), function(g)
    list(N0 = N0_e,
         returns = simulate_group(om, N0_e, om$X_assumed, PHI_E, NMIX_E,
                                  trip_size = 1, stochastic = TRUE)))
  fit_multi(gs, om, mode = "flag0", nmix = NMIX_E,
            interval = intervals_e[[interval]])
}, by = .(rep, cell, N0_e, interval)]

res_e[, `:=`(rel_bias = F_hat / om$F_true - 1,
             interval = factor(interval, levels = c("default", "wide")))]

# Summary statistics, in the order they should be read: a bounded tail
# frequency first, then the mean the Jensen argument speaks to, then the
# median for comparability, then the diagnostic that says whether the mean can
# be taken at face value.
summarise_e <- function(d) {
  d[, .(tail_frac = mean(F_hat > E_TAIL_MULT * om$F_true),
        tail_mcse = sqrt(mean(F_hat > E_TAIL_MULT * om$F_true) *
                         (1 - mean(F_hat > E_TAIL_MULT * om$F_true)) / .N),
        mean_bias = mean(F_hat) / om$F_true - 1,
        mean_mcse = stats::sd(F_hat) / sqrt(.N) / om$F_true,
        bias      = median(rel_bias),
        mcse      = mcse_median(F_hat) / om$F_true,
        bound_pct = 100 * mean(at_bound),
        n         = .N), by = .(N0_e)][order(N0_e)]
}

summ_e      <- summarise_e(res_e[interval == "default"])
summ_e_wide <- summarise_e(res_e[interval == "wide"])

knitr::kable(
  summ_e[, .(N0_e, tail_frac, tail_mcse, mean_bias, mean_mcse,
             bias, mcse, bound_pct, n)],
  digits = 4,
  col.names = c("Tags per group", paste0("P(F-hat > ", E_TAIL_MULT, "x truth)"),
                "MCSE (tail)", "Mean rel. bias", "MCSE (mean)",
                "Median rel. bias", "MCSE (median)", "% at bound", "n"),
  caption = paste0("flag0 against release-group size, at psi = ",
                   round(psi_of(om, PHI_E, NMIX_E), 3),
                   " (phi = ", PHI_E, ", nmix = ", NMIX_E,
                   ", one release group), over the default search interval."))
