Boundary contact is not negligible: at the smallest group size 4.2% of replicates return an estimate sitting on an endpoint of the default interval. The mean at that cell is therefore a censored quantity, and the wide-interval column is the one to read. Widening the interval moves the mean at the smallest group size by +7.3%, against a joint Monte Carlo standard error of 29.5%, so the mean is stable to the choice of ceiling. The gross-overshoot frequency moves by +0.2% — as it should, since the threshold of 5\(\times\) the truth lies far below either ceiling — which is why it is the statistic carried into the summary sections.

Code 
# Three statistics on a shared x axis, free y scales, so the tail frequency is
# not squashed by the scale of the mean. One ggplot rather than a stacked
# layout, to avoid a package dependency the rest of the document does not have.
e_panel <- rbind(
  summ_e[, .(N0_e, stat = paste0("P(F-hat > ", E_TAIL_MULT, "x truth)"),
             val = tail_frac, mcse = tail_mcse)],
  summ_e[, .(N0_e, stat = "Mean relative bias",
             val = mean_bias, mcse = mean_mcse)],
  summ_e[, .(N0_e, stat = "Median relative bias",
             val = bias, mcse = mcse)])

e_panel[, stat := factor(stat, levels = c(
  paste0("P(F-hat > ", E_TAIL_MULT, "x truth)"),
  "Mean relative bias", "Median relative bias"))]

ggplot(e_panel, aes(N0_e, val)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = val - 2 * mcse, ymax = val + 2 * mcse),
                 alpha = 0.7, colour = pal[["flag0"]]) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7, colour = pal[["flag0"]]) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, colour = pal[["flag0"]]) +
  facet_wrap(~ stat, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  # Break at the design points rather than at decade-ish defaults, which label
  # values the design never visits and leave the smallest group on the panel
  # edge.
  scale_x_log10(breaks = sort(unique(e_panel$N0_e)),
                labels = scales::comma,
                expand = expansion(mult = 0.07)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Tags per release group (log scale)", y = NULL)

At 125 tags per group, 6.0% of replicates — 24 of 400 — return an estimate of \(F\) more than 5 times the truth; at 10,000 the figure is 0.0%. The difference is +6.0% against a joint Monte Carlo standard error of 1.2%, so the two ends of the design are separated by more than two joint standard errors. The corresponding difference in the mean is +91.7% against a joint standard error of 20.0%, which is also resolved and, per the interval check above, is not an artefact of the ceiling.

Across the design the correlation with \(\log N_0\) is -0.67 on the overshoot frequency and -0.71 on the mean. The median behaves differently — its correlation is 0.52 — but the median at the smallest group size is not distinguishable from zero (-4.8%, against a Monte Carlo standard error of 25.0%), so it carries no information about the effect in either direction. The honest reading is that the median is blind to this effect, not that it contradicts it. That is what the mechanism predicts. A convex inversion applied to a noisier target moves probability mass into the right tail; it does not shift the bulk of the distribution the same way, so the centre stays where it was while the mean is dragged upward by the minority of groups that report many returns during mixing. Any diagnostic that looks only at the middle of the distribution will see nothing at all, when what is actually happening is a heavy right tail.

The effect is resolved, and it runs in the direction the convexity argument predicts. That makes release-group size a third condition on the default’s unbiasedness, independent of the reporting rate and the survival floor: the deterministic inversion is unbiased in the large-sample limit, not in general. The form the failure takes is a tail rather than a shift – at 125 tags per group roughly one release group in 17 returns an estimate more than 5 times the truth, while the median at that cell is not distinguishable from zero – so assessments built from many small release groups should not expect the Experiment B robustness result to hold at face value, and should not expect a median-based diagnostic to warn them.

The three statistics have to be read together, and none of them is sufficient alone. At 125 tags per group the median is not distinguishable from zero, the mean is +91.7%, and the overshoot frequency is 6.0%. A single small release group can therefore look unremarkable on a median-based diagnostic while contributing a large upward pull to a pooled estimate. The mean overstates the typical group, the median conceals the tail entirely, and the frequency is the statistic that says what a reader of a real assessment should actually expect to encounter: not that every small group is biased, but that some fraction of them are badly so. The obvious lever is the assumed reporting rate: at fixed \(N_0\), a lower \(X_{assumed}\) thins \(R_t\) directly and inflates the divisor, attacking both sides of the ratio at once. That is listed under Suggested extensions rather than run here, because the low-\(X\) region is also where the survival floor engages, and separating the two mechanisms needs a design that holds the floor inactive by construction.

Note that this experiment isolates group size from the survival floor — the reporting rate is correct, so the raised target is correct on average and the floor is not the operative mechanism. In a real configuration the two run together, and small groups make floor engagement more likely as well.

What the results show

1. When the assumed reporting rate is right, flag0 is unbiased and flag1 is not — and this holds across the whole Experiment B configuration space. flag0 recovers \(F\) regardless of \(\varphi\) and nmix (largest absolute median bias 2.7%), because the deterministic inversion never needs to know how available tagged fish were. flag1 asserts \(X = 1\) during mixing, which is false for every tagging programme ever run; its bias in \(F\) is downward, meaning biomass biased upward, reaching -63% in the worst cell, and it worsens steeply as either the mixing period lengthens or tagged fish become more vulnerable. tag_flags(i,2) = 1 is a robustness choice, not a correctness fix, and it errs optimistically.

Experiments C and E qualify this heavily. The unbiasedness of flag0 survives a reporting rate that is correct only on average rather than group by group, and it survives clumped reporting provided the survival floor does not engage. Where it does — low assumed reporting rates, high availability — flag0’s median bias reaches -36%, because a capped removal is an under-removal and under-removal is flag1’s error. Experiment E adds a third condition: the result is a large-sample one, and it degrades at realistic release-group sizes. The claim that the default is unbiased holds only inside a region of configuration space, and that region shrinks as assumed reporting rates fall.

2. The reporting rate, not the flag, is the first-order channel — except at high availability. The forward estimator handles mixing correctly but keeps \(X\) fixed at the wrong value, so the gap between it and flag0 measures what the mixing treatment contributes over and above the reporting-rate error. Across the low-availability part of the design that gap is small: at \(\varphi = 0.5\) it never exceeds 2.7%, and outside the true > assumed column it never exceeds 0.4%. A wrong reporting rate rescales every predicted return in the informative periods too, not just the mixing ones, and that channel dominates.

The exception matters. The largest gap in the design is 63%, at \(\varphi = 2\), nmix = 4, true > assumed — +139% for flag0 against +76% for forward. Where tagged fish are highly available during a long mixing period, the deterministic removal stops being a second-order correction and becomes a large error in its own right. So the flag is not always the minor channel; it is minor in the regime the mixing period was designed for (\(\varphi < 1\)) and major in the regime that is arguably more realistic for purse-seine tagging. Experiment C shows the same boundary in a different coordinate: the gap is negligible where the floor is inactive and first-order where it is not. Attributing a biomass shift entirely to the flag will not survive a sensitivity run, but nor will dismissing it without knowing where in \(\varphi\) the fishery sits.

3. The two flag settings form a one-sided interval and cannot bracket the truth when the assumed reporting rate is too high. Because \(X_{assumed} < 1\), flag0 always removes more tags than flag1 and always returns the larger \(\hat{F}\); the interval therefore has flag0 as its upper end. It can only contain the truth when flag0 sits above it, which happens only when the true reporting rate is at or above the assumed value. Across the entire 27-cell design, bracketing never occurs in any replicate whenever the true rate is below the assumed one. Where bracketing does occur it is either degenerate (true = assumed, where flag0 is simply unbiased and noise straddles the truth roughly half the time) or genuine but extremely wide (high \(\varphi\), true > assumed, intervals up to 1.8 times \(F\)).

Implication for grid design: running tag_flags(i,2) at 0 and 1 as alternative levels spans an assumption; it does not bound the truth, and the direction in which it fails to bound depends on the sign of the reporting-rate error — which is exactly the thing under dispute. If the real uncertainty is in the reporting rate, that is what belongs on the grid.

4. Longer mixing periods amplify a reporting-rate error under every estimator except forward_X. This is a correction to an expectation worth stating explicitly, because the intuition that “the forward model turns excluded data into information, so longer mixing should help” is not what the simulation shows. At \(\varphi = 2\) with the rate underestimated, flag0 runs +68% → +139% as nmix goes 2 → 4. But forward degrades too (+55% → +76% over the same range), because fixing \(X\) at the wrong value contaminates the extra mixing-period observations just as it contaminates the post-mixing ones. Adding data does not help when the added data are being scored against a misspecified nuisance parameter.

Only forward_X, which lets \(X\) move, is flat in nmix (+1% → +1%). The lesson is that handling the mixing period as a likelihood is necessary but not sufficient; the benefit only materialises when the reporting rate is estimable. Any sensitivity to tag_flags(i,1) in a real assessment should be read as partly a reporting-rate sensitivity in disguise.

5. Only estimating the reporting rate fixes the misspecification. forward_X recovers \(F\) to within 4.9% in 26 of the 27 cells of Experiment B — 23 of 27 at a 4% threshold — and recovers \(\varphi\) at all three values tested. The two largest residuals are +5.4% (nmix = 4, phi = 1, true = assumed) and -4.9% (nmix = 2, phi = 2, true < assumed), each within 2.2 Monte Carlo standard errors of zero, against a typical MCSE for this estimator of 1.9% — forward_X is much the noisiest of the four, so its worst cells are where noise would be expected to show. The structural reason it works at all is that under flag0 and flag1 the reporting rate deterministically rewrites the tagged population and the data have no mechanism to object; under the forward parameterisation the mixing-period returns become evidence about \(X\) rather than an instruction. Note the caveat in the Limitations: this vignette identifies \(X\) far more cleanly than MULTIFAN-CL could.

6. The default’s failure mode is real, and it is triggered by low assumed reporting rates in combination with high availability, not by uncertainty in the rate. The floor engages when the realised catch fraction in a mixing period exceeds \((1-\tau)X_{assumed}\), about 0.78 times the assumed rate under MULTIFAN-CL defaults — a fifth easier to reach than the exhaustion condition \(C_t/N_t > X_{assumed}\) that the obvious reading of the manual suggests. At an assumed rate of 0.5 with \(\varphi = 1\) that is not reached in this design; at 0.5 with \(\varphi = 2\) it is reached in 3–67% of replicates, and at 0.2 with \(\varphi = 2\) in 57–100%.

Trip-level clumping amplifies this but is not required for it. Small release groups and stochastic recaptures are sufficient on their own: with trips taking only 1% of a release group — effectively independent reporting — the floor still engages in 17% of replicates at \(X_{assumed} = 0.2\), \(\varphi = 1\), and 57% at \(\varphi = 2\). This matters for how the result is defended: clumping is the ingredient an unsympathetic reader will call contrived, and the finding does not depend on it. An assessment that revises its tag-seeding estimates downward moves itself into this regime without changing anything else.

7. Under floor engagement, the default degenerates into the alternative. Where the floor rarely engages, clumped reporting costs flag0 precision but not accuracy — the median stays within 4% while the interquartile range roughly doubles. Where it routinely engages, flag0 loses accuracy too, and in the same direction as flag1: once posfun caps the removal the default cannot remove the number of tags its own rule demands, so it under-removes and \(F\) is biased downward (median -36% at \(X_{assumed} = 0.2\), \(\varphi = 2\)). The practical consequence is that the two settings are not as different as they look in the regime where the choice matters most. Neither behaviour would be visible in standard assessment diagnostics, which is an argument for checking the floor condition directly rather than inferring it from fit statistics.

8. flag1’s bias is a function of one measurable quantity. The mixing-period recapture fraction \(\psi\) collapses \(\varphi\) and nmix onto a single axis, and the analytic approximation \(-(1-X)\psi N_0 / (N_{post} + (1-X)\psi N_0)\) tracks the simulation closely (correlation 0.998). This makes the question empirical rather than general: compute \(\psi\) from the .tag file and the expected downward bias in \(F\) follows — a few percent at \(\psi = 0.05\), roughly a third of \(F\) at \(\psi = 0.3\), more than half at \(\psi = 0.5\).

9. The likelihood-based treatment is not free. forward_X recovers \(F\) and \(X\) cleanly in Experiments A and B, where one release group of 10,000 tags carries the information. In Experiment C’s more realistic configuration — eight groups of 500 — it is the widest of the four estimators in 89% of cells and its median wanders over -46% to +35%. Structural correctness does not substitute for information: estimating the reporting rate, the availability multiplier and \(F\) together needs data that a fragmented tagging programme may not provide. This tempers the recommendation in point 5, and it is a reason to treat a code change as a medium-term improvement rather than a fix available to the current assessment.

10. Release-group size is a structural assumption. Experiment E shows the default’s unbiasedness is a large-sample property: inverting a noisy target is convex in the target, so small release groups put weight in the upper tail of F even when the reporting rate is correct and the floor is inactive. At 125 tags per group, 6.0% of groups return an estimate more than 5 times the truth, against 0.0% at 10,000, while the median at the small-group cell is not distinguishable from zero. The failure is a tail, not a shift, which is why it is invisible to the diagnostics an assessment normally reports. Release-group size is not usually treated as an assumption worth stating; on this evidence it is one.

What to check in an assessment that fits to tags

This is the practical residue of the five experiments, in the order it is worth working through. It sits here rather than in the executive summary because every figure it refers to has been produced by the time it renders, so the numbers below are read from the fitted objects rather than transcribed.

1. Which setting was used, and whether it was held constant. tag_flags(i,2) was inert in MULTIFAN-CL until version 2.2.7.6 (July 2025), so any comparison against an earlier assessment involves a model change rather than a like-for-like retrospective. “They used the default” describes the behaviour correctly but not a decision anyone made — the alternative did not exist. A change of setting between a draft and a final model would move biomass in a predictable direction and should be documented as a structural choice, not a bug fix.

2. The assumed reporting rates, and the direction of any revision. This is the first-order channel through most of the design: at \(\varphi = 0.5\) the gap between the deterministic treatment and a correctly specified forward model never exceeds 2.7%. A downward revision of tag-seeding estimates raises inferred \(F\) and lowers biomass through the ordinary likelihood, and separately pushes the model toward the regime where the default breaks down. The two effects compound and are easily conflated. The exception is high availability during a long mixing period, where the flag becomes a first-order channel in its own right (largest gap in the design 63%, at \(\varphi = 2\), nmix = 4). For the 2026 bigeye assessment the values and the direction of revision are both documented: SC22-SA-IP-05 gives purse seine reporting-rate priors with means of 0.496 in region 2, 0.512 in region 3 and 0.528 in region 4, each between 15 and 24 per cent below what the 2023 assessments would have used under the same region and fishery definitions, with the reduction driven largely by the introduction of double-tag effects. Read those as penalty distributions rather than fixed values — the model estimates the rate against them — and note that they cover purse seine fleets only, that the region 2 penalty was deliberately halved to reflect additional uncertainty, and that the region 2 prior is not recommended for the Indonesian and Philippine domestic fisheries.

3. Whether the survival floor is engaging. The floor engages when the realised catch fraction in a mixing period exceeds \((1-\tau)X_{assumed}\), about 0.78 times the assumed rate under MULTIFAN-CL defaults — that is 0.390 at an assumed rate of 0.5 and 0.156 at 0.2, which ordinary fishing mortalities reach. When it happens, posfun silently caps the removal and the default then under-removes, biasing \(F\) downward and biomass upward — the same direction as the alternative it is supposed to improve on. In MULTIFAN-CL the floor is set by age_flags(118) and (119), with a penalty weighted by age_flags(117)/1e8; if age_flags(117) < 0 the penalty weight is zero and the rescaling leaves no trace in the objective function at all. Check age_flags(117), (118) and (119), and check whether age_flags(198) (release-group-specific reporting rates) is active, which makes the divisor vary by group.

4. The mixing-period recapture fraction \(\psi\). For tag_flags(i,2) = 1 the downward bias in \(F\) is largely governed by this one measurable quantity: the proportion of each release group recaptured within tag_flags(i,1) periods of release. The .tag file records reported returns rather than recaptures, so the returns have to be raised before dividing:

\[\hat\psi_i \;\approx\; \frac{1}{X} \cdot \frac{\sum_{t \le \texttt{tag\_flags}(i,1)} R_{it}}{N_i}.\]

Omitting the \(1/X\) returns \(X\psi\) rather than \(\psi\), which at a reporting rate near 0.5 halves the diagnosed fraction — and because the bias steepens with \(\psi\), it understates the consequence by more than half again. Then read the bias off Experiment D or evaluate \(-(1-X)\psi N_0 / (N_{post} + (1-X)\psi N_0)\) directly: -4.8% to -3.9% at \(\psi = 0.05\); -33.4% to -27.7% at \(\psi = 0.3\); -59.9% to -50.9% at \(\psi = 0.50\). Each range is printed worst-first, and because a longer mixing period carries the worse bias at a given \(\psi\) — the ordering the Experiment D tripwire guards — the worst end is the longest mixing length. Take that end where tag_flags(i,1) is large. Two caveats: \(\hat\psi\) inherits any error in the reporting rate it is raised by, in the direction that understates the problem; and a release-group-weighted mean aggregates over groups whose mixing lengths differ. This is an afternoon’s work against the .tag file and it turns a general argument into a specific one about that assessment’s data.

5. The size of the release groups. The default inverts a noisy observation, and that inversion is convex in the observation, so small release groups put weight in the upper tail of \(F\) that the large-sample argument does not predict. At 125 tags per group, 6.0% of release groups return an estimate more than 5 times the truth with the reporting rate correct and the floor inactive, against 0.0% at 10,000. Note that the median at the small-group cell is not distinguishable from zero: the cost is a heavy right tail across release groups, not a shift every group shares, so it will not show up in a diagnostic built on medians. Count the releases per group in the .tag file and check how much of the tagging data sits in groups of a few hundred.

6. Whether the flag appears as a grid axis, and how it is described. Running both settings spans an assumption; it does not bound the truth. The pair is structurally one-sided — the default always returns the larger \(F\) — so it can never bracket when the assumed reporting rate is too high, and where it does bracket the interval reaches 1.8 times the quantity being estimated. If the real uncertainty is in the reporting rate, that is what belongs on the grid.

Guidance on tag_flags(i,2)

Neither setting of tag_flags(i,2) is correct, and the choice between them should be made and reported as a conditional one.

Simulation testing shows that the default, tag_flags(i,2) = 0, recovers fishing mortality without appreciable bias when the assumed tag reporting rate is correct, across all combinations of mixing-period length (2–4 quarters) and tagged-fish availability (\(\varphi\) = 0.5–2) tested in Experiment B. That robustness is structural: the deterministic inversion solves for whatever mixing-period fishing mortality reproduces the implied removal, so it does not require the availability of tagged fish during mixing to be correctly specified.

It is, however, conditional on further requirements, and the claim should not be extended past the design in which it was demonstrated. Where the realised catch fraction in a mixing period exceeds roughly four-fifths of the assumed reporting rate, the raised removal drives the tagged population below the survival floor, the floor engages, and the default then under-removes — biasing fishing mortality downward by as much as 36% in our tests. This condition is reached routinely at assumed reporting rates around 0.2, and at 0.5 whenever tagged fish are substantially more available during mixing than the general population. The default’s reliability therefore declines precisely as reporting-rate estimates are revised downward — and they are being revised downward. The purse seine reporting-rate priors for bigeye in SC22-SA-IP-05 have means of 0.496 to 0.528 across regions 2 to 4, between 15 and 24 per cent below the values the 2023 assessments would have used under the same region and fishery definitions. The 2026 bigeye assessment therefore sits at the boundary of this condition, not safely inside it, and a further revision of the magnitude just observed would move it across. Separately, the result is a large-sample one: at 125 tags per release group, 6.0% of release groups return an estimate of fishing mortality more than 5 times the truth even with a correct reporting rate and an inactive floor, while the median at the same cell is not distinguishable from zero. The cost is a heavy right tail across release groups rather than a shift each group shares, so it is invisible to a median-based check and it does not average away as quickly as pooling suggests.

The alternative, tag_flags(i,2) = 1, assumes complete reporting during the mixing period. This is not true of any tagging programme, and the resulting bias is systematic rather than conservative: fishing mortality is underestimated and biomass correspondingly overestimated, with the error growing as either the mixing period lengthens or tagged fish become more available. Under plausible configurations the bias in fishing mortality reached 63%. Its one merit is predictability — the bias is largely a function of the proportion of each release group recaptured during the mixing period, which is computable from the .tag file in advance provided the reported returns are raised by the assumed reporting rate first. The qualifier matters in both directions: the recapture fraction does not determine the bias entirely, since at a fixed fraction a longer mixing period is worse by 9.1% at the top of the range tested; and an analyst who forgets the raising will diagnose half the fraction and conclude the setting is far cheaper than it is.

On balance the default remains preferable where reporting rates are moderate, tagged-fish availability during mixing is not elevated, the survival floor is demonstrably not engaging, and release groups are large enough for the large-sample argument to apply. All four conditions should be checked and reported rather than assumed. Neither setting protects against misspecification of the reporting rate itself, which is the larger error channel in most cases examined; the two settings do not bracket the truth and should not be used as alternative levels in a structural uncertainty grid. Where reporting rates are uncertain, that uncertainty should be represented directly.

The treatment that would resolve the dilemma rather than manage it is to predict mixing-period returns and score them in the likelihood, with the reporting rate estimated against its tag-seeding prior. MULTIFAN-CL cannot currently do this — mixing-period returns do not enter the tag likelihood under either setting — so it is a request to the MULTIFAN-CL development team rather than something an assessment can configure. We recommend it as a medium-term change, with the caveat that the simulation here also shows it is not free: with many small release groups it was the least precise of the four estimators tested, under a prior looser than any assessment would impose.

Because both settings are biased and the choice is unavoidable in any model fitted to tags, we further recommend that a configuration omitting tagging data — with spatial structure carried by a fleets-as-areas approach — be included in the structural uncertainty grid. This bounds the influence of the tag data on stock status without requiring the mixing-period treatment to be resolved first, and it answers a question of direct management relevance: how much of the assessment result depends on the tagging programme. This recommendation follows from the demonstrated deficiencies of both flag settings rather than from any simulation of a spatial model, which is outside the scope of this vignette.

Limitations

This is a deliberately stripped-down operating model and it flatters the forward model in ways a real assessment would not.

  • The number of tags released is known exactly, and there is no abundance, selectivity, movement, or catchability to confound with the reporting rate. Identification of \(X\) here is far stronger than in MULTIFAN-CL, where \(X\) trades off against \(q\) and against absolute abundance. The extent to which forward_X rescues a bad prior is therefore optimistic, and the prior standard deviation (0.4 on the log scale) is loose. Tightening it toward a hard tag-seeding constraint moves forward_X back toward forward.
  • \(\varphi\) is a single scalar applied uniformly across the mixing period. In reality availability presumably decays smoothly from release, and varies by fishery. A step function is the simplest possible caricature.
  • No spatial structure. The reason a mixing period exists at all is that effort is not randomly distributed relative to release sites; that spatial process is represented here only through its effect on \(\varphi\).
  • Observation error. Experiments A, B, D and E use unclumped reporting; Experiment C adds trip-level clumping but the likelihood remains Poisson, whereas MULTIFAN-CL offers negative binomial and binned options via parest_flags(111). Fitting a likelihood matched to the clumping would narrow the dispersion penalty seen in Experiment C.
  • The posfun analogue is approximate, and its penalty does no work. The smooth floor and quadratic penalty reproduce the qualitative behaviour of do_newton_raphson_for_tags() — catch capped, survival floored — but it is not a transcription of the MULTIFAN-CL code, and the weight is set by hand rather than derived from age_flags(117). More importantly, because the mixing target depends only on the data and not on any parameter, the penalty is constant with respect to the parameter vector and cannot influence \(\hat{F}\). That makes this vignette a faithful model of the age_flags(117) < 0 case specifically. A configuration with a positive penalty weight might behave differently, and nothing here tests that.
  • Clumping is modelled as a single trip size. Real reporting varies by fleet, and a mixture of well-reporting and non-reporting fleets would behave differently from a homogeneous trip process with the same mean. At the coarsest trip setting the realised number of trips per release group per period falls to a handful, so that corner of the design should be read as an extreme rather than as a typical fishery.
  • The forward estimators are not tuned for the Experiment C sample size. forward_X estimates three parameters from eight groups of 500 tags under a loose prior; its poor performance there reflects that configuration rather than a defect of the parameterisation. A tighter prior, more release groups, or fewer free parameters would all improve it, and this vignette does not locate the boundary.
  • Experiment C fixes the mixing length at nmix = 3. Experiment B’s claim of robustness across mixing lengths is therefore not re-tested under the realistic observation model.
  • Experiment E resolves a difference, not a curve, and the mean it reports is not a bias correction. The design separates the smallest and largest release-group sizes by 6.0% in overshoot frequency, against a joint Monte Carlo standard error of 1.2%, which establishes that group size matters but does not pin down the functional form between the two ends. The mean at the smallest group size is driven by a small number of extreme replicates and carries a large standard error of its own (20.0%); it is stable to a large widening of the search interval, but it remains a statistic about a tail and should be read as evidence of one rather than as a number to subtract off an assessment. The solved F is unbounded above in principle, so any mean of it is conditional on a bound imposed by the analyst – which is a general property of the deterministic inversion, not an artefact of this simulation. Release-group size also varies total tags alongside group size, so precision varies across the design, which is why every statistic is reported with its own Monte Carlo standard error.
  • No spatial or fleets-as-areas configuration is simulated. The recommendation to include a tag-free branch in a structural uncertainty grid follows from the demonstrated deficiencies of both flag settings, not from any result in this document.
  • \(\psi\) is treated as known. In practice it would be estimated from observed recaptures, which are themselves thinned by the reporting rate, so a real calculation would need to raise them — reintroducing some of the uncertainty the exercise is trying to characterise.

Suggested extensions

  • Replace the Poisson observation model with a negative binomial and estimate the dispersion, to see how much of the contrast survives realistic overdispersion.
  • Let \(\varphi\) decay geometrically with quarters at liberty rather than switching off at nmix, and estimate the decay rate. This is closer to the biology and would show whether tag_flags(i,1) needs to be a sharp boundary at all.
  • Add multiple release cohorts with \(\varphi\) grouped by quarter at liberty — the structure that makes \(\varphi\) identifiable in a real model, and worth demonstrating before proposing it to the developers.
  • Sweep the prior standard deviation on \(X\) in forward_X, and treat this as the highest-value outstanding run in this list. The value used throughout is 0.4 on the log scale. The penalty parameters in SC22-SA-IP-05 imply coefficients of variation on the bigeye purse seine reporting rate of roughly 0.05 to 0.09 — close to an order of magnitude tighter than the prior imposed here. forward_X was the least precise estimator tested in this document, and that finding is one of the reasons given for treating a likelihood-based treatment as a medium-term development request rather than a current option. Until the sweep is run it is not possible to say how much of the imprecision is intrinsic to the estimator and how much is an artefact of a prior far looser than any assessment would impose. The sweep would also locate where the ability to revise the reporting rate is lost, which is the other half of the trade-off.
  • Fit with nmix misspecified relative to the truth, since in practice the analyst chooses tag_flags(i,1) without knowing the real mixing time.
  • Add a forward variant with \(\varphi\) fixed at 1. The current flag0–forward gap conflates two changes — scoring the mixing-period returns in the likelihood, and adding a free availability parameter — so it does not cleanly isolate the mixing channel.
  • Give the survival-floor penalty something to act on, by making the mixing-period target depend on an estimated quantity, and check whether a positive age_flags(117) changes the Experiment C conclusions.
  • Establish what bounds the solved \(F\) in MULTIFAN-CL. In this vignette the deterministic inversion is unbounded above and is held in check by an explicit search interval, which is why every tail statistic here is reported against a boundary-contact diagnostic. A real implementation has its own effective bound — through parameter bounds on \(F\), through the survival floor, or through the Newton solver’s own failure behaviour — and which of these binds first determines what an extreme release group actually does to an assessment. Reading that out of the code would say whether the tail found in Experiment E is realised as a large \(\hat{F}\), as a floored removal, or as a convergence failure the analyst would notice.
  • Vary nmix within Experiment C, to test whether Experiment B’s robustness across mixing lengths survives the realistic observation model.
  • Push the noise-to-signal ratio through \(X_{assumed}\) as well as through release-group size, to separate the two routes into the same mechanism. A lower assumed rate thins \(R_t\) and inflates the divisor simultaneously, so it attacks the ratio harder than \(N_0\) can alone, and it is the axis a real assessment moves along when seeding estimates are revised. The complication is that the low-\(X\) region is also where the survival floor engages, so the design would need to hold the floor inactive by construction — a large \(N_0\) with a low \(\varphi\), or the floor disabled outright — to attribute any effect to the inversion rather than to the cap. Done properly this would also pin down the functional form that Experiment E establishes the existence of but does not resolve.
  • Raise the replicate count in Experiment E and add intermediate group sizes. The present design establishes that the two ends differ but leaves the shape between them unresolved, and a tail frequency is an inherently noisy statistic: its Monte Carlo error scales as \(n^{-1/2}\), so halving the resolvable difference from the present 2.4% costs four times the replicates. That is affordable here, since the flag modes are one-dimensional, and it is what would turn the third condition from a qualitative warning into something an analyst could calibrate against their own release-group sizes.
